name: Livoletide

lead: Livoletide is an experimental peptide designed to curb the extreme hunger of Prader-Willi syndrome. Fat-loss followers watch it as an appetite lever: less hunger, lower intake, a leaner body.

It mimics unacylated ghrelin, a form of the hunger hormone that does not activate the usual ghrelin receptor, and it was meant to replace a reported relative shortage of that form in people with PWS. Its main phase 2b/3 trial (ZEPHYR, 158 participants) is recorded as terminated, and no study has tested it for appearance-related fat loss.

paras: It has only been used in clinical trials for hyperphagia in Prader-Willi syndrome. There is no consumer routine, and no data exist on how long any change would take in people seeking cosmetic fat loss.

It is investigational and has never been approved. Safety information comes from nonclinical and juvenile toxicity work and trial records. It was developed for a rare medical condition, and its effects in people without that condition are unknown.

web.title: Millendo stops livoletide development for PWS after failure in pivotal ZEPHYR trial
Millendo's livoletide fails in pivotal trial for Prader-Willi syndrome

angle.text: Livoletide is an investigational appetite peptide that acts like unacylated ghrelin to turn down hunger, which in theory means lower intake and a leaner body. It was built for hunger in Prader-Willi syndrome, and its pivotal trial was terminated.

lead: Livoletide (AZP-531) is a cyclic peptide analogue of unacylated ghrelin, a form of the hunger-related hormone ghrelin, developed to treat hyperphagia, the intense and persistent hunger, in Prader-Willi syndrome (PWS).[1][2] Its relevance to appearance is through body weight and fat: appetite drugs that reduce food intake are the mechanism by which people lose fat, and the compound is sometimes grouped with experimental weight and appetite peptides, because it targets the ghrelin system that drives hunger and fat storage.[3] It was designed for a rare genetic disorder rather than for cosmetic use.

Early human studies tested it in healthy, overweight or obese people and people with type 2 diabetes, where it was developed to improve glycaemic control and reduce weight, and then in people with PWS.[4][5] Its pivotal phase 2b/3 trial, ZEPHYR, enrolled 158 participants; in April 2020 the developer, Millendo Therapeutics, reported that the phase 2b part did not show a statistically significant improvement over placebo on its primary hunger endpoint and stopped the programme.[6][7][8] It has not been approved, and no study has tested it for cosmetic fat loss in people without PWS.

Livoletide is a useful reference point for how the ghrelin system is approached as a drug target: ghrelin is produced mainly in the stomach, its level rises before meals, and in animals ghrelin and mimetics raise body weight and fat mass, which is why the pathway attracts attention from people interested in appetite and body composition.[3] The unacylated form that livoletide imitates was studied as a counterweight to that signal rather than a blocker of its receptor.[2]

paras: Prader-Willi syndrome is a rare genetic disorder caused by loss of function of genes on the paternal copy of chromosome 15. Most cases involve a deletion of the paternal region, a smaller share involve two maternal copies of the chromosome, and the rest involve imprinting defects.[9] Estimates of incidence range from about 1 in 10,000 to 1 in 30,000 people.[9] Infants have weak muscle tone and feeding difficulty; from roughly age 2 to 8, persistent hunger develops that often leads to severe obesity and type 2 diabetes, and caregivers commonly restrict access to food.[9] Management at the time of the livoletide programme centred on supervised diet, activity, growth hormone for children and behavioural support.[9] The FDA approved diazoxide choline for hunger in the condition in March 2025.[9]

Ghrelin was identified after its receptor was characterised in 1999 and takes its name from its role in releasing growth hormone. The enzyme GOAT attaches an octanoic acid chain to ghrelin, and only this acylated form activates the main ghrelin receptor. The unacylated form does not activate it but has separate effects, including on appetite and liver glucose output.[3] Acylated ghrelin peaks before meals and injected ghrelin increases food intake; in animal studies ghrelin and mimetics raise body weight and fat mass. Obese people generally have lower ghrelin levels, with Prader-Willi syndrome the notable exception.[3] This is the biological context for livoletide: it is an analogue of the unacylated form, intended to oppose acylated ghrelin rather than block its receptor.[2][4]

PWS is a rare genetic disorder in which infancy is marked by feeding difficulty and a later stage brings hyperphagia and obesity. At the time the livoletide programme was described there was no approved treatment for the hyperphagia.[1][10] Livoletide's intended use was to reduce hyperphagia and food-related behaviours in people with PWS.[10]

Acylated ghrelin is an appetite-stimulating hormone that also promotes fat storage and affects glucose metabolism. A 2013 review explained that unacylated ghrelin and its analogues were shown to inhibit plasma acylated ghrelin levels and improve glucose metabolism, and described AZP-531 as a cyclized fragment of unacylated ghrelin in development for type 2 diabetes and PWS.[2] People with PWS have been reported to have elevated acylated ghrelin and a relative deficit of unacylated ghrelin, which underlies the hypothesis that replacing it reduces hyperphagia.[4][10]
In a phase 1 study, maximum concentrations were typically reached about one hour after subcutaneous dosing, exposure was dose-proportional, and the mean terminal half-life was 2 to 3 hours.[5]

Livoletide has not been approved in any jurisdiction. Its pivotal phase 2b/3 ZEPHYR trial, which began in March 2019 with 158 participants, is listed as terminated on ClinicalTrials.gov.[6][11] Nonclinical and juvenile toxicity work presented at endocrine meetings supported its development in children and adults with the condition.[10][12][13]

Millendo Therapeutics announced topline ZEPHYR results on 6 April 2020, with trade coverage dated the following day. Participants aged 4 to 65 were randomised to one of two livoletide dose levels or placebo as a daily subcutaneous injection for 12 weeks. The hunger questionnaire score (HQ-CT) improved in all arms, including placebo, by 2.8 points on placebo versus 4.7 and 3.8 points on the low and high dose; the differences were not statistically significant on the primary or secondary measures.[7][8] The treatment was generally well tolerated, with mostly mild injection-site reactions as the most common adverse events; two participants stopped livoletide, and four reported serious adverse events that were not judged related to treatment.[7] Following these results Millendo stopped the phase 3 portion and the nine-month extension study, redirecting resources to its programmes in congenital adrenal hyperplasia and menopausal hot flashes, and its shares fell about 70 percent on the news.[7][8]

Prader-Willi hunger remained a target for other developers afterwards; the FDA approval of diazoxide choline in March 2025 is the first approved drug for hyperphagia in the condition, according to the encyclopedia entry on the syndrome.[9]

Livoletide appears in discussions of experimental fat-loss peptides because it acts on appetite hormones, in the same broad area as other ghrelin-pathway and incretin-pathway compounds. All human work on it has been in healthy, overweight or diabetic volunteers in early safety studies and in people with Prader-Willi syndrome.[4][5] Its earlier phase 1 programme described it as designed to improve glycaemic control and reduce weight, which is the link people draw to body composition.[5]

A 2017 study found that AZP-531 reduced infarct size in a mouse model of myocardial ischemia and reperfusion.[14] A 2020 eLife paper reported that unacylated ghrelin and AZP-531 suppressed growth of breast cancer cells in three-dimensional culture and xenografts; this is laboratory work only.[15] Nonclinical and juvenile toxicity studies were presented at endocrine meetings.[10][12]

Phase 1: a three-part randomized study in healthy subjects (n=44), overweight or obese subjects (n=32) and patients with type 2 diabetes (n=36) tested single and multiple subcutaneous doses against placebo for up to 14 days; AZP-531 was well tolerated and pharmacokinetics were dose-proportional.[5]

Prader-Willi syndrome, phase 2: a multicenter randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial enrolled 47 patients with genetically confirmed PWS and hyperphagia, who received daily subcutaneous injections of AZP-531 or placebo for 14 days. The drug was well tolerated, and the total, 9-item and severity-domain scores on the Hyperphagia Questionnaire improved significantly compared with placebo (p below 0.05).[4] A conference abstract reported improvement in hyperphagia and food-related behaviours in both obese and non-obese people with PWS.[10]

Phase 2b/3: the ZEPHYR randomized, placebo-controlled trial (NCT03790865), started in March 2019 with 158 participants, is listed as terminated.[6][11] No study of livoletide for cosmetic weight or fat loss was found.

ZEPHYR results (April 2020): in the 12-week randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled phase 2b part, livoletide did not produce a statistically significant improvement over placebo in hyperphagia and food-related behaviours; the earlier 14-day phase 2 trial had reported improvements on the same type of questionnaire, and the larger, longer trial did not reproduce them at the primary endpoint.[4][7][8] The registry lists the study as terminated for that reason.[6]
